questions.why: A call pays max(0, price − strike), minus the premium: {answer}.

questions.why: A put pays max(0, strike − price), minus the premium: {answer}.

questions.q: Match each derivative to what it does.
pairs: Agree now to buy or sell at a fixed price on a future date
The right, not obligation, to buy at the strike
The right, not obligation, to sell at the strike
Exchange fixed-rate payments for floating-rate ones
questions.why: Futures lock in prices, options buy rights, swaps exchange payment streams.

questions.q: An airline buys fuel futures to fix next year's fuel cost. What is it doing?
options: Hedging: reducing a risk it already has
questions.why: It already faces fuel price risk; the futures offset it, swapping uncertainty for a known cost.

questions.q: What's the most the buyer of an option can lose?
questions.why: Buyers have a right, not an obligation, so the worst case is letting it expire and losing the premium.

questions.q: Someone who sells a call option without owning the shares has a limited maximum loss.
questions.why: If the price shoots up, they must deliver shares they don't own at the strike: losses have no upper limit.

questions.q: A company has a floating-rate loan and fears rates will rise. Which swap helps?
options: Pay fixed and receive floating, effectively fixing its interest cost
Buy a call option on shares
Sell its loan to a hedge fund
questions.why: The floating payments it receives cover its loan's floating interest, leaving it paying fixed.

questions.q: Match each event to what happened.
pairs: One trader's hidden futures losses broke the bank
Sold huge amounts of credit default swaps and needed a rescue
LDI strategies forced to sell gilts as yields jumped
Stand between both sides and collect collateral daily
questions.why: Leverage, complexity and counterparty risk are the common threads; clearing was part of the fix.

questions.q: A CFD on a trading app is a derivative.
questions.why: Its value comes from the underlying price; you don't own the asset. Most retail CFD accounts lose money.

questions.q: Explain the difference between using a derivative to hedge and using it to speculate.

ideas.label: Hedging reduces a risk you already have (like a farmer or airline)
Speculating is betting on a price move to make a profit, adding risk

questions.model: Hedging uses a derivative to reduce a risk you already face, like an airline fixing its fuel cost or a farmer locking in a wheat price. Speculating uses it to bet on a price move to make a profit, which adds risk rather than reducing it.

tests.answer: Hedging reduces a risk you already have, like an airline fixing fuel prices; speculating is betting on a price move to make money.

questions.q: Explain why derivatives can lead to huge, sudden losses.

ideas.label: They're often leveraged, so small price moves cause big losses
They're complex or hidden, so risks are hard to see (and the other side may not pay)

questions.model: They're often leveraged, so a small move in the underlying can mean a huge loss. They can also be complex and hidden, so risks build up unseen, and if the other side can't pay, losses spread from firm to firm.
questions.why: Leverage plus complexity is a dangerous mix.

tests.answer: They're leveraged so small moves create big losses, and they're complex and hidden so nobody sees the risk building up.
